0. Preface

In this note, I talk about deep learning based language models. I try to present the model as mathematically concise as possible and along the way motivate the terms involved. We start with neural networks and walk our way until we get to transformer-based language models, the model used in the making of ChatGPT. At the end, I explain my thoughts on why these things work, and pose some questions that I think are important. I also try to show the coding part of all these, and for this, I use PyTorch.

I think Artificial Intelligence is one of the most consequential technologies in our lifetime. It is different from other technologies in that it is not too hard to learn. It has so many potential uses and misuses. So it is important that enough good people know it and, hopefully, we can steer it in a good direction that is beneficial to all. And to be able to do something with this technology, we need to at least understand the models and be able to implement it. In fact, this note grows out of a class I am teaching to several friends in Cambodia, with the goal of improving language models for Khmer, my native language. The current note is the second version of the note. I upgraded the first version while preparing lecture notes for a class on natural language processing that I teach at the Institute of Technology of Cambodia. The hope is to build a team that can facilitate and accelerate the development and deployment of large language models in Cambodia.

I recommend the reader to read the "theory part" to get conceptual understanding first, and then proceed to read the code to try to implement it.

1. Artificial Neural Network

Let's imagine that our body receives a signal, say through the eyes. This signal goes through the eyes and flows from one group of neurons to the next until it reaches a certain place where we make a certain judgement about the signal, say whether it is a cat or a flower. How to make a mathematical model of this process?

Let x be a signal. After receiving the signal, the input signal x goes to a first group neurons N11,N21,..,Nk11, neurons in the first layer, each Ni1 processes information it received and passes it to deeper group of neuron N12,...,Nk22, neurons in the second layer, this process continues until the signal reaches a certain depth L with neurons N1L,...,NkLL, neurons in the L-th layer, and the result from these last group combined to produce an output.

The simplest way to model a neuron Nji processing its inputs is to add all the inputs it receives to get a single number. However, a neuron has different connection with other neuron, so instead of doing ∑xki−1, we do weighted sum ∑wk,jixki−1. So here wk,ji captures the strength of connection of neuron Nki−1 at layer i−1 with neuron Nji at layer i. The weighted sum can be seen as dot product between the weighted vector Wji=(w1,ji,w2,ji,…,wki−1,ji)T and the output of layer i−1 vector Xi−1=(x1i−1,…,xki−1i−1)T, we have xji=(Wji)TXi−1.

w1,jiw2,jiwki−1,jiNeuron N1i−1Neuron N2i−1Neuron Nki−1i−1Neuron Njilayer i−1layer i
x1i−1x2i−1xki−1i−1Xi−1=w1,jiw2,jiwki−1,jiWji=xjilayer i−1layer i

The weight vector Wji represents the strength of connection neuron Nji has to those in layer i−1. The total output of layer i−1 is packed into a vector Xi−1. For other neurons in layer i, they have their weight vector Wmi, and the signal it gets from layer i−1 is also represented as a dot product of Xi−1 with the weight Wmi−1. So the output of layer i is a vector

Xi=[(W1i)TXi−1⋮(Wkii)TXi−1]=[(W1i)T⋮(Wkii)T]Xi−1=[w1,1iw2,1i⋯wki−1,1iw1,2iw2,2i⋯wki−1,2i⋮⋮⋱⋮w1,kiiw2,kii⋯wki−1,kii]Xi−1

We represent the collection of weighted vectors as the matrix Wi=[W1i,…,Wkii]T, so Xi=WiXi−1. So we see that starting from input, which is represented as a vector X0, the neurons in the first layer produce X1=W1X0, and this input gets fed to the neurons in the second layer to produce X2=W2X1 and so on. We obtain a dynamical system {X0=inputXi+1=Wi+1Xioutput of neuron layer i+1

X0
X1=W1X0
X2=W2X1
⋯
XL=WLXL−1

Now there is an issue, XL=WLXL−1=WL(WL−1XL−2)=⋯=(WL⋯W1)X0, but the product of matrices WL,WL−1,…,W1 gives another matrix, call it W, i.e., XL=WX0. What this means is we can think of the whole process as just one layer from X0 to XL with one matrix multiplication.

To give a sense of multi-layers, we need to go back to examine how information is transmitted in between two neurons. Let's say we have neuron A transmit information to neuron B. A doesn't continuously send information to B, there is a gap in their synaptic connection.

A only sends information to B if it has enough information. What this means is that there is a gate between the synaptic connection and this gate opens when certain condition is met. This phenomenon happens in other places in nature too. For example, we have a ceiling that water seeps in. The water doesn't continuously drip down because there is surface tension, so it accumulates until gravity has enough strength to pull it down.

bxReLu(x−b)

To model this gate phenomenon, we use a function called rectified linear function ReLu:R→R defined by ReLu(x)=x if x is positive and ReLu(x)=0 if x≤0. This function acts as a gate: it only allows information to pass forward if it is greater than 0. Now we want to allow a neuron to have its own threshold other than 0. So for neuron Nji, it has a threshold bji. And the gate function is ReLu(x−bji). This mechanism is called self gate.

To apply this gating process to a layer of neurons, we use bias vector bi=(b1i,…,bkii)T and the dynamical equation above is upgraded to {X0=inputXi+1=ReLu(Wi+1Xi+bi+1) where the ReLu is applied component wise to the vector Wi+1Xi+bi+1.

The gate function is often called activation function since we can think the neuron gets activated when the threshold is reached. In the n dimensional space Rn, the map from Rn to Rm given by L(x)=Wx with W an m by n matrix is called a linear map. The collection of these maps is denoted by L(Rn,Rm), and this can be shown to be equal to the set of m by n matrices Mm×n. The map A(x)=Wx+b is called affine map, it generalises the line equation y=ax+b in one dimension. The gate/activation function is usually denoted by σ.

Definition

A neural network is a function obtained by composing affine linear functions with non-linear functions. More precisely, a neural network of L layers is a function NN:Rn→Rm defined by NN(x)=AfL∘σL−1∘⋯∘Af2∘σ1∘Af1(x) where each Afi:Rki−1→Rki is an affine map, i.e., Afi(x)=Wix+bi, with Wi∈L(Rki−1,Rki) and bi∈Rki and k0=n and kL=m. Each σi is a non-linear function applied pointwise to the output of Afi.

Let me clarify what we mean by "applied pointwise" here. Say we have a function f(x):R→R, and v=(v1,v2,..,vN) is a vector. Applying f on v pointwise is f(v)=(f(v1),f(v2),...,f(vN)).

The model without gate treats the flow of information as continuous, while the one with gate takes into account that information can stop propagating if it doesn't have enough energy.

The picture we should have in mind of a neural network is a collection of neurons ordered as layers, and between them there are connections, and each neuron has a threshold associated to it, usually known as bias. The vector bi is called bias vector. The strength of connection between neurons is kept in the matrix Wi. Below is the picture we should have in mind where the strength of connection is labeled with color from blue to red.

X0X1X2X3X4W1W2W3W4
−11

The structure of the neural network, i.e., how many layers there are and how many neurons in each layer, together with the choice of the activation function is called the architecture of the neural network.

The ReLu(x−b) function with threshold b decides if x>b, it will send the input forward, and if not, it doesn't. There is no middle ground. This is known as hard gate. To get a soft gate, people use SiLu(x−b)=(x−b)sigmoid(x−b), where sigmoid(x)=ex/(1+ex) is a number between 0 and 1, so the input is let through partly. Below is the graph of the hard gate and our new soft gate.

bx
hard gate ReLu(x−b) soft gate SiLu(x−b)

The reason we call it soft gate is that when x is large, sigmoid(x) is approximately 1, so SiLu(x)∼x×1=x. And when x is very small (in negative sense) sigmoid(x)∼0, so SiLu(x)∼0. However, when x is close to 0, the SiLu(x) is not just 0 as we see in ReLu(x).

People also use sigmoid function, tanh, and others as activation function. sigmoid(x)=ex1+ex,tanh⁡(x)=ex−e−xex+e−x,softplus(x)=ln⁡(1+ex)

sigmoid(x)
tanh⁡(x)
softplus(x)

1.1 Coding Neural Networks with PyTorch

One popular Python Package used in deep learning is PyTorch, developed by Facebook, where we now turn to. Coding will be introduced throughout this note layer by layer.

In Python, when you want to use a package or a library, you have to import it. The package that we need now are matplotlib.pyplot, used to plot graphs, and pytorch, used to create tensors. To import, write the following in the code block.

import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

The basics object in PyTorch are tensors, which are multi-dimensional arrays. There are quite a number of ways to create PyTorch tensors, and we recommend the reader to read the PyTorch documentation for detail. Here we only show a few examples to give an idea of how it works.

a=torch.tensor([-1,2]) # create a tensor from a list of numbers from package torch
b=torch.tensor([2,-7])

We can perform operation on tensors.

  1. a+b define pointwise addition
  2. 3*a perform pointwise multiplication
  3. b**2 perform pointwise square
import torch
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt#  shorten matplotlib.pyplot to plt
a = torch.linspace(-4, 4, 30)# create a tensor of 30 elements of numbers evenly spaced between -4 and 4
plt.plot(a,a**2-3*a) #            plot a^2-3a on a axis 
plt.title('graph of a^2-3a') 
plt.xlabel('a')
plt.ylabel('a^2-3a')
graph of a^2-3a
a^2-3a against a

Once you create a tensor, you can slice it or sample various subsets of it. We show a few ways of how this can be done.

x=torch.rand(2,3) #    this create a tensor of 2 by 3 whose elements are random number between 0 and 1
x1=x[1,:]         #    we define a tensor x1 to be the second row of x
y1=x[:,2] 
#Now we can print the above tensors 
print(f'x= {x}')
print(f'x1={x1}')
print(f'y1={y1}')
x= tensor([[0.9607, 0.1908, 0.6339],
        [0.9940, 0.0890, 0.3960]])
x1=tensor([0.9940, 0.0890, 0.3960])
y1=tensor([0.6339, 0.3960])

x=[x11x12x13x21x22x23]∈R2×3,x1=(x21,x22,x23),y1=(x13,x23)

Python counts from 0, so x[1,:] is the second row and x[:,2] is the third column. In PyTorch, x1 and y1 are lists of numbers of shape (3,) and (2,); the row and the column above show which entries we picked.

To create neural network, we can use package torch.nn from PyTorch. To get this package, we need to import it

import torch.nn as nn

Once we have torch.nn, we can create affine function by torch.nn.Linear(n,m).

import torch.nn as nn
L=nn.Linear(2,3) # this create an affine map taking 2 dimensional input and output 3 dimension

In mathematical term, we create L(x)=Wx+b, where W is a 3 by 2 matrix and b∈R3. The entries of W and b are random number. If we want the bias term b=0, we can do L=nn.Linear(2,3,bias=False). The code nn.Linear(2,3) produce an object that has several attribute and operation attached to it.

W=L.weight
b=L.bias 
print(f'Weight W of L: {W}')
print(f'Bias b of L: {b}')
Weight W of L: Parameter containing:
tensor([[-0.2916, -0.7016],
        [ 0.3956,  0.5720],
        [ 0.3072,  0.3156]], requires_grad=True)
Bias b of L: Parameter containing:
tensor([-0.6838, -0.4431, -0.2809], requires_grad=True)

W=[w11w12w21w22w31w32]∈R3×2,b=[b1b2b3]∈R3,L(x)=Wx+b,x∈R2

nn.Linear(2,3) takes a vector in R2 to R3, so W has 3 rows and 2 columns, which is the shape PyTorch prints. This is our notation from section 1, Xi=WiXi−1 with Wi∈Rki×ki−1. PyTorch itself computes xWT+b with x written as a row, which gives the same numbers.

Let's me explain a bit more about L=nn.Linear(n,m). Sure it creates a linear map L∈L(Rn,Rm). But this is something created for using in machine learning, and during training a neural network, it is efficient to process several data points, called batch, at the same time. So the natural input for L is a batch of vectors instead of a vector, ie it expects the input of shape [batch_size,input_dim]. Say we have a batch of vectors [v1,v2,...,vk], where vi∈Rn, then the linear map

L=nn.Linear(n,m)

processes this stack in parallel and produce [L(v1),...,L(vk)]. We will get back to this more later. When we create L, what we get is an object. In Object-Oriented Programming (OOP), an object has attributes and methods. I tend to think of attribute as internal state or data of the object, and methods are functions or action we can do with these internal states or datas. The objectnn.Linear(n,m) has weight W and bias b attached to it, that's expected. What more is that the weight W is a pair (weight,gradient) not just the weight, same for b.

v1vkL(v1)L(vk)LW∈Rm×nb∈Rmv1,…,vk∈Rn[k,n]L=nn.Linear(n,m)L(v1),…,L(vk)∈Rm[k,m]

Let's create a two layers neural network N:R→R, obtained by composing a affine map A1:R→R20, tanh, and A2:R20→R.

class NeuralNet(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):           #  this is the part where we define attribute inside object NeuralNet
        super().__init__()        #  this initializes the base class nn.Module
        self.A1=nn.Linear(1,20)   #  create A1 as an affine map from 1d to 20 dim
        self.A2=nn.Linear(20,1)
    def forward(self,x):          #  this is where we assemble all part/attribute of NeuralNet 
        y=self.A1(x)
        y=torch.tanh(y)
        y=self.A2(y)
        return y
N = NeuralNet()                   #  this create a neural network

N=Af2∘tanh∘Af1: R→R20→R,Af1(x)=W1x+b1,W1∈R20×1, b1∈R20,Af2(h)=W2h+b2,W2∈R1×20, b2∈R

self.A1 and self.A2 are the affine maps Af1 and Af2 of the definition, and torch.tanh is the activation function σ, applied pointwise. Writing N(x) calls the method forward, which is where this composition is written.

Now we can plot what function our neural network produce.

x = torch.linspace(-20, 20, 300)  # create domain
with torch.no_grad():             # this code is there to stop pytorch from keeping track of derivative
    y = N(x.view(-1,1))           # the 300 points as a stack of shape [300,1], processed at once

#plot the result
plt.figure(figsize=(10,5))
plt.plot(x, y)
plt.show()

We will see how to train a neural network after we learn stochastic gradient descent.

2. Digression: Metric Spaces

Distance is a quantitative method that allows us to say how close or far two things are to each other. In space R2 or R3, we have distance formula given by Pythagorean theorem

Distance from A to B=(a1−b1)2+(a2−b2)2

A=(a1,a2)B=(b1,b2)|b1−a1||b2−a2|distancea1a2

This formula also has an analogue in higher dimension, where now we have points A=(a1,…,an) and B=(b1,…,bn) in Rn, and

Distance from A to B=(a1−b1)2+(a2−b2)2+⋯+(an−bn)2=∑i=1n(ai−bi)2

d(x,y)≤d(x,z)+d(z,y)

In mathematics, distance is not only restricted to locations, but it is between two objects. For example, we have distance between two numbers a and b defined as |a−b|. It is very important to be able to say when two things are similar or close to each other in an objective manner. To do this, we need to talk about metric space. What this means is that we can find a way to measure distance between objects of interest even if they are not locations as we conventionally think about. Let us denote the collection of objects we study as X. Our goal is to find a way to measure distance between two points x1 and x2 of X. This distance is denoted by d(x1,x2). We say d is a metric if it satisfies the following conditions

  1. d(x,y)≥0, and d(x,y)=0 if and only if x=y.
  2. d(x,y)=d(y,x).
  3. d(x,y)≤d(x,z)+d(z,y).

The first condition just means that if x and y are different points, their distance must be greater than 0, and distance between x and x itself is 0. The second condition says distance is symmetric, meaning distance from x to y is the same as from y to x. The third is known as triangle inequality and it means that if you travel from x to y by detouring to z first, then you increase your traveling path.

The Euclidean distance that we talk about satisfies these three conditions. First note that distance

d(A,B)=(a1−b1)2+(a2−b2)2.

Proof of 1 and 2. Both terms (a1−b1)2 and (a2−b2)2 are ≥0, so the sum is ≥0 and so is its square root. If d(A,B)=0, then a sum of two terms that are ≥0 equals 0, so both terms are 0, that is a1=b1 and a2=b2, and A=B. If A=B, both terms are 0 and d(A,B)=0. This is condition 1. For condition 2, (a1−b1)2=(b1−a1)2 and (a2−b2)2=(b2−a2)2, so d(A,B)=d(B,A).

The proof of the triangle inequality of property 3 is a bit more involved and we prefer not to give it here.

ABd2(A,B)=5d1(A,B)=4+3=7

Now I want to point to the fact that there is more than one way to measure distance. Imagine you try to build an app similar to Grab. If you measure distance using a straight line as the Euclidean distance does, the driver would not be happy because that is not how they drive their tuk-tuk. They drive their tuk-tuk based on the grid streets of the city. So it makes more sense to measure distance that way. This gives rise to what is known as taxicab metric, denoted by

d1(A,B)=|a1−b1|+|a2−b2|.

To give a notation for the Euclidean metric, we denote it by d2.

Beside the metrics d1 and d2, we have a more general notion of metric denoted by

dp(A,B)=(|a1−b1|p+|a2−b2|p)1/p

for any p≥1. These metrics satisfy all the desired properties 1, 2, 3 we mentioned earlier.

In this course, our object of interest is function. Consider a function f:[−1,1]→R. And we have another function g:[−1,1]→R. We want to have a way to say they are close to each other. People have come up with several ways of doing this. One approach is they look at the gap between the two functions at each point, and the largest gap is called the distance. In particular they define

d(f,g)=maxx∈[−1,1]|f(x)−g(x)|.

−11xfgd(f,g)

The collection of continuous functions from [−1,1] to R is denoted by C[−1,1]. Together with distance d∞(f,g)=maxx∈[−1,1]|f(x)−g(x)|, C[−1,1] is a metric space. What this means is that we can study when two functions are close to each other or not. This is important to us because we want to approximate a function we need, so we must have some way to tell us when two functions are close or not. More generally, if X is a nice subset of Rd, we can study continuous functions from X to R, or Rn, and the collection of these functions, denoted by C(X), forms a metric space with the metric

d∞(f,g)=maxx∈X‖f(x)−g(x)‖.

Another metric on C[−1,1] is the density of area bounded by the two curves. In particular, given f and g in C[−1,1], we define

d1(f,g)=12∫−11|f(x)−g(x)|dx.

−11xfgd1(f,g)=12×shaded area

More generally, for f and g in C(X), we define

d1(f,g)=1area(X)∫X‖f(x)−g(x)‖dx.

One important notion in metric space is density. A subset A of X is called dense in X if we can approximate any element of X by members of A, i.e., for any x in X and any ε>0, we can find a in A such that d(x,a)<ε. We see an example of this with the rational numbers Q being dense in R. We know a great deal about the rational numbers and we can even represent them in the computer. However, we don't know most elements of R and we can't represent them in any computer. The famous example is π, the ratio of the circumference and the diameter. This is a very important number, people have been studying it since ancient times, and it appears almost everywhere in science and engineering. To have access to it, we use its rational approximation 3.14, or a longer decimal if we need to be more accurate, and we can make it as accurate as we like since Q is dense in R.

Like R, we don't know most functions in C(X). Our goal is to find a suitable candidate like Q to approximate elements in C(X). By this time, you should realise that anything in the world can be represented as a function, for example the future is the output of the present, therefore if we can approximate any function, we can even predict the future. In the next section, we will see that the set N of neural networks can approximate any function in C(X) if X is a cube. This means that N is dense in C(X).

3. Universal Approximation Theorems

A neural network is defined by its weight matrices Wi and bias vectors bi, collectively known as parameters and denoted by P=(W1,W2,…,WL,b1,…,bL). These parameters can be thought long vector of dimension K for some K∈N, representing a point P in RK. Each point corresponds uniquely to a neural network instance, denoted NNP, which is structured according to the network's fixed architecture. This parameter-to-network mapping can be expressed as: P↦NNP The primary task of machine learning is to select the parameter P that make NNP best approximates the function of interest. This point of view allow us to see ML is a technique of function approximation much like that of Fourier series and Taylor expansion.

R2P=(a1,a2)P↦ReLu(a1x+a2)C([−1,1])ReLu(a1x+a2)−11

One obvious question is what kind of function can be approximated by neural networks. The answer of this question coming from universal approximation theorems which we are now turn to. First, we look at a theorem due to G. Cybenko in his paper Approximation by Superpositions of a Sigmoidal Function

Universal Approximation Theorem, G. Cybenko: The space N2=⋃N=1∞{∑iNαiσ(yiTx+bi)∣yi∈Rd} is dense in C(Id,R), where σ:R→R is a fixed discriminatory function, to be defined below, and Id is the unit cube in dimension d.

Here dense is in the sense of Section 2 with the metric d∞. For any f in C(Id,R) and any ε>0, we can find g in N2 such that d∞(f,g)<ε, that is |f(x)−g(x)|<ε for every x in Id.

Definition We say that σ is discriminatory if for a measure μ∈M(In), ∫Inσ(yTx+θ)dμ(x)=0 for all y∈Rn and θ∈R implies that μ=0.

Proof

Note that N2=⋃N=1∞{∑iNαiσ(yiTx+bi)∣yi∈Rd} is a linear subspace of C(Id,R). Assume it is not dense, then its closure N2― is a proper Banach subspace of C. We can define a linear functional ℓ:N2―→R to be zero. Since N2― is a proper subspace, the Hahn-Banach's theorem allows us to extend ℓ to all of C such that ℓ(f)=0 if f∈N2― and ℓ(f)≠0 for some f∉N2―. In particular, there exist f0∈C such that ℓ(f0)≠0.

Now follow Riesz-Markov-Kakutani representation theorem, we know there exist a signed Borel's measure μ on Id such that ℓ(f)=∫fdμ for all f∈C. In particular ∫σ(yiTx+b)dμ=0 for all y∈Rd and b∈R. But σ is discriminatory, this implies μ=0. However, we know that ∫f0dμ=ℓ(f0)≠0, this is a contradiction.

The next stage of the proof is to prove that the activation functions we have above are discriminatory with respect to the Lebesgue measure. This is true but we won't be proving it here.

We can equip the space C(Id,R) with the Lp norm, and there are similar results by Kurt Hornik in 1990 in his paper Approximation capabilities of multilayer feedforward networks.

Theorem, K. Hornik: The space N2=⋃N=1∞{∑iNαiσ(yiTx+bi)∣yi∈Rd} is dense in the space of C(Id,R) when C is equipped with the Lp norm with 1≤p≤∞ and σ is a continuous, bounded and non-constant function.

The Lp distance is dp(f,g)=(1area(Id)∫Id|f(x)−g(x)|pdx)1/p, and area(Id)=1. For p=1 this is the metric d1 of Section 2. So Cybenko's theorem is density in d∞ and Hornik's theorem is density in dp.

3.1 Implementation

Let's consider the task of finding a two-layer neural network to approximate cos⁡(x) for x∈[−10,10] with respect to the L2 norm. Given ε>0, the Universal Approximation Theorem tells us that there exists a neural network which is ε-close to cos⁡(x) on this interval in the L2 norm. The question then is which neural network? Unfortunately, there is no straightforward way to identify it directly. What we can do is fix an architecture for the network and then search for the parameters P that work best. We start with a random initial guess for P and use gradient descent to iteratively improve this guess.

Let's set this mathematically. As an example, first, we select the architecture by setting the first layer to have dimension 13 and the second layer to have dimension 5.

R1R13R5R1W1W2W3

This means we are looking for a function NNP(x)=W3(σ(W2σ(W1x+b1)+b2))+b3 where W1 is a matrix that takes R1 to R13, W2 is a matrix taking R13 to R5, W3 is a matrix that takes R5 back to R, and b1∈R13,b2∈R5 and b3∈R. In this case, P=(W1,W2,W3,b1,b2,b3) is a point in R13⋅1+13⋅5+5⋅1+13+5+1=102.

Given P∈R102, we construct a function NNP(x) to approximate the cosine function. The error of this approximation is measured by the loss function, defined as: loss(P)=∫−1010(cos⁡(x)−NNP(x))2dx Note that loss(P)=20d2(cos,NNP)2, where d2(f,g)=(120∫−1010|f(x)−g(x)|2dx)1/2 is the L2 distance on [−10,10]. So making the loss small means making NNP close to cos in this metric. The task is to optimize loss:R102→R. Of course we can't hope to find P that truly is the minimum since the dimension is so large. What we can hope for is to find P such that loss(P)<ε for an acceptable ε>0.

Next, we need to be more realistic. We cannot compute loss(P) directly because the function NNP(x) is difficult, if not impossible, to integrate analytically. To address this issue, we define a loss function at each point as: l(P,x)=|cos⁡(x)−NNP(x)|2 and then approximate the overall loss function loss(P) by: loss(P)≈lossD=∑i=1Nl(P,xi)N where D={x1,…,xN} is a set of points sampled from [−10,10]. Here, the subscript D indicates a loss function depends on the data set D. Since this loss function is based on the data, it is called the empirical loss. Note that as N→∞, by continuity, lossD(P)→120loss(P)=d2(cos,NNP)2.

Let's summarize where we are now. We have a dataset D. For each data point xi∈[−10,10], we can evaluate the point-wise loss for each parameter set P. Averaging these, we obtain the empirical loss: lossD(P)=∑i=1N|cos⁡(xi)−NNP(xi)|2N While this empirical loss is computable, it remains challenging to optimize using critical points method. A method commonly used for this optimization is called gradient descent.

4. Gradient Descent Algorithm

Let's remind ourselves what gradient descent is. Consider f:Rd→R. The goal is to find a point P where f(P) is the global minimum of f. The gradient descent algorithm suggests the following steps:

  1. Start at a point P0.
  2. Compute the gradient ∇f(P0).
  3. Take a small step η>0 in the direction opposite to the gradient, i.e., P1=P0−η∇f(P0).
  4. Repeat the above process.

The number η is known as the learning rate. The reason we move in the direction opposite to the gradient is that the function decreases fastest in this direction.

k = 37
f(Pₖ) = 0.6171

We now state and prove that if f is a nice function, the gradient descent algorithm will converge to a minimum. Note that most function we encounter in machine learning are far from being nice.

Theorem Let f:Rd→R be a strongly convex, bounded below, non-constant differentiable function where the derivative Df:Rd→Rd of f is Lipschitz. Then f has a unique minimum, we denoted it by Pc. Moreover, for η sufficiently small, the sequence Pn+1=Pn−η∇f(Pn) converges to Pc for any initial point P0.

Definition Let f:Rd→R. We say f is convex if for all P,Q∈Rd and λ∈[0,1] we have f(λP+(1−λ)Q)≤λf(P)+(1−λ)f(Q), which implies f(P)−f(Q)≥∇f(Q)T(P−Q) if f is differentiable. A function f is strongly convex if there exist μ>0 such that f(P)≥f(Q)+∇f(Q)T(P−Q)+μ2‖P−Q‖2. And F:Rd→Rd is Lipschitz if there exist L>0 such that ‖F(P)−F(Q)‖≤L‖P−Q‖ for any P,Q∈Rd.

Note: If f is convex, with Df being Lipschitz doesn't imply uniqueness of a minimum, f(x,y)=x2 is an example of such function.

Proof Recall that the gradient descent update rule is given by: Pk+1=Pk−η∇f(Pk) where η is the step size (learning rate). We aim to show that this sequence Pk converges to the global minimum.

Since f is strongly convex, there exists a constant μ>0 such that for any P and Q, f(Q)≥f(P)+∇f(P)T(Q−P)+μ2‖P−Q‖2.

Using the Lipschitz continuity of ∇f, we also have that there exists L>0 such that: ‖∇f(P)−∇f(Q)‖≤L‖P−Q‖.

Now, consider the difference in function values at consecutive points in the gradient descent sequence. The Lipschitz continuity of ∇f gives: f(Pk+1)≤f(Pk)+∇f(Pk)T(Pk+1−Pk)+L2‖Pk+1−Pk‖2.

Substitute Pk+1=Pk−η∇f(Pk) into this inequality: f(Pk+1)≤f(Pk)−η‖∇f(Pk)‖2+Lη22‖∇f(Pk)‖2. This simplifies to: f(Pk+1)≤f(Pk)−(η−Lη22)‖∇f(Pk)‖2. For convergence, we require η to satisfy η<2L. In this case, the term η−Lη22 is positive, and thus f(Pk+1)≤f(Pk), implying that the function values decrease with each iteration of gradient descent.

Since f(P) is bounded below, the sequence f(Pk) converges, say to mf.

The equation f(Pk+1)≤f(Pk)−(η−Lη22)‖∇f(Pk)‖2. can be rewrite as 0≤(η−Lη22)‖∇f(Pk)‖2≤f(Pk)−f(Pk+1)

Sum up above expression from k=0 to N, we obtain

0≤(η−Lη22)∑k=0N‖∇f(Pk)‖2≤f(P0)−f(PN+1)≤f(P0)−mf

This means the series ∑k=0∞‖∇f(Pk)‖2 is convergent, and therefore ∇f(Pk)→0 as k→∞.

Finally, we use strong convexity. Let Pc be the minimum of f. And this we leave it for keen readers to entertain themselves to prove that it exists and is unique. Since Pc is the minimum, ∇f(Pc)=0. Apply the strong convexity inequality with (P,Q)=(Pc,Pk) and with (P,Q)=(Pk,Pc): f(Pk)≥f(Pc)+μ2‖Pk−Pc‖2,f(Pc)≥f(Pk)+∇f(Pk)T(Pc−Pk)+μ2‖Pk−Pc‖2. Adding the two inequalities and using the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, we get μ‖Pk−Pc‖2≤∇f(Pk)T(Pk−Pc)≤‖∇f(Pk)‖‖Pk−Pc‖. Therefore ‖Pk−Pc‖≤1μ‖∇f(Pk)‖→0, that is, Pk converges to Pc.

4.1 Stochastic Gradient Descent

Consider the problem of training a neural network NN(x) to learn a function F:R→R. We don't know F but we have N samples of it, i.e., the data of F. Let D={(x1,y1),(x2,y2),...,(xN,yN)} be the data we collect about F.

Let's say we fix a neural network architecture, in other word, we fix the number of layers and the number of neuron the neural network has. This specification dictates the size of parameter P. Let's say P∈RK. Then the empirical loss function lossD(P)=∑i=1N|F(xi)−NNP(xi)|2N=∑i=1N|yi−NNP(xi)|2N This is a function from RK→R. Training the neural network means using the gradient descent, GD ,to update the parameter P. Now if N is large, the loss function for the whole data set can be computationally costly and the network can overfit the data. Stochastic gradient descent is proposed to solve these issues. Instead of computing the loss function for all N data points, we instead compute it on subset of size n where n is much smaller than N.

Now fix n<N, the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is as follow:

  1. Select random n data points from D, this make D~⊂D.
  2. Form loss function with respect to D~, lossD~(P).
  3. Use gradient descent to update P.
  4. Select new n data points from D randomly, call it D~ again.
  5. Form lossD~(P).
  6. Update P using gradient descent.
  7. Repeat the above step.

The number n used to compute the stochastic loss function is call batch size. Let's suppose we have N=1000 data points, if we make batch size n=20, then goes through all data points we must run the SGD 1000/20=50 times. When we run through all the data, people say it is an epoch.

Remark: An interesting question is how do we know that evolution of Pk via SGD algorithm converge to a stable position, let alone a global minimum.

4.2 Training Neural Networks with PyTorch

Let's say we want to find a neural network to approximate cos⁡(x) on I=[−20,20]. First, we create a data of cosine value on I, and then train a fixed size two layers neural network to approximate this data.

#Import libraries
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy

#Generate data of cosine
x=torch.linspace(-10,10,200)
y=torch.cos(x)                   # pytorch cosine function apply pointwise on a vector
plt.figure(figsize=(10,3))
plt.plot(x,y)

Next, we create a neural network with 3 layers. The input starts with 1 dimension, passes through a 40-dimensional space, then a 15-dimensional space, and finally maps to a 1-dimensional output (a real number).

# Define a model
class NeuralNetwork(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super(NeuralNetwork,self).__init__()
        self.A1=nn.Linear(1,40)
        self.A2=nn.Linear(40,15)
        self.A3=nn.Linear(15,1)
    def forward(self,x):
        y=torch.tanh(self.A1(x))
        y=torch.tanh(self.A2(y))
        y=self.A3(y)
        return y
net=NeuralNetwork()
W1b1W2b2W3b380+615+16=711
# plotting the network before training
z=torch.zeros(len(x))
with torch.no_grad():
    for i in range(len(x)):
        z[i]=net(x[i:i+1])
plt.figure(figsize=(10,4))
plt.plot(x,z)
#Define loss function
def loss_fn(a,b):
    return (a-b)**2
#choose learning rate
lr=0.01
# Start gradient descent step
for _ in range(40000):
    idx = torch.randint(0, len(x), (1,)).item()      # select a random index between 0 and size of x
    input=x[idx:idx+1]                               # get the point x corresponding to the index selected above
    output=y[idx]                                    # get the value of cosine 
    predicted_out=net(input)                         # value computed by the neural network
    loss=loss_fn(predicted_out,output)               # compute the error 
    net.zero_grad()                                  # make the gradient associate to parameter in net to be zero
    loss.backward()                                  # compute the gradient for any parameter used when computing loss
    with torch.no_grad():                            # stop tracking gradient
        for param in net.parameters():
            param.data -= lr * param.grad
            
# Now evaluate how the model changed after training
with torch.no_grad():
    predicted_by_net=net(x.view(-1,1))
plt.figure(figsize=(12,3))        
plt.plot(x,y,label='Cosine')
plt.plot(x,predicted_by_net,label='NeuralNet')
plt.xlabel('Input')
plt.ylabel('Output')
plt.title('Cosine vs NeuralNet')
plt.legend()

Note that our batch size is 1. That's why I wanted the network to do gradient descent 40000 steps.

One might think that the network "learn" the cosine function. I think this is not the case, I think what the network does is it imitate the data it see and that's all to it. Let's plot the neural network prediction in a domain larger than what it've seen.

x_l=torch.linspace(-20,20,1000) # create a larger domain 
y_cos=torch.cos(x_l)
with torch.no_grad():
    y_net=net(x_l.view(-1,1))
plt.figure(figsize=(13,3))
plt.plot(x_l,y_cos,label='Cosine')
plt.plot(x_l,y_net,label='NeuralNet')

Cosine  NeuralNet

An easy argument to see that a neural network defined above can never approximate the cos⁡(x) on R regardless how big it is is that a neural network has only finitely many critical points while the cosine function has infinitely many critical points.

Now, let's me explain about the zero_grad issue. In PyTorch, when we create an tensor W, it could come as a pair (W,grad). And this is always true for parameter in neural network objects. For example, in the neural network we defined above, there are several parameters. If we do net.A1, this will give us a linear map nn.Linear(1,40), which is an object on its own. Now when we do net.A1.weight, we get the weight of A1, and associate to this weight is grad. This mean we have a pair (W,grad). The code loss.backward(), compute the derivative of the loss function, and it updates gradient of any parameters that involve in computing the loss function, therefore W will get its gradient updated. In the beginning, before the gradient is updated at all, grad=0, and loss.backward() update the gradient by accumulation, i.e., 0+grad. Note that this doesn't change the weight W itself. To change W, we must do gradient descent. After the gradient descent, the pair (W,grad) become (W_new,grad). Next if we do loss.backward() again, we would get a pair (W_new,grad+grad(W_new)), so to avoid this problem, we need to make the pair (W_new,grad) to (W_new,0) first before we do loss.backward(), and we can do this by net.zero_grad(), which set gradients of all parameter to be zero.

Below we train a neural network, with the same data, batch size 1, learning rate 0.01 and 40,000 steps. The heat maps show every weight and bias of the network, teal for negative and red for positive, and the darker the colour, the larger the number. The graph on the right shows cos and the network. Under them, the loss is the mean squared error over the 200 points, and the norm of each weight and bias is its length, ‖W‖=∑ijWij2. When you train, the neural network becomes closer to cosine and the loss goes down. At the same time, a few rows of W2 and the cells of W3 change colour, and the norms of W2 and b1 grow, while the norm of W1 stays almost the same.

5. Recursive Language Models

A sentence is a string of words and a language is a collection of sentences. We let Σ be the set of words spoken in a language. Denote by Σ∗ the set of all finite sentences, whether they make sense or not. The language L is the set of sentences that are spoken or written, this means L⊂Σ∗. Note that we haven't yet defined what spoken means and what counts as a word. For now we can treat Σ as just a set, and a language as a collection of strings of symbols we find when we observe a language. In this point of view, a sentence is whatever string of symbols we find in the wild and a language is the collection of those strings. The benefit of this general and somewhat abstract approach is that it allows us to see anything as a language.

Let us look at some examples.

Example 1. First, we can think of Khmer documents as a language. Whatever has been written or spoken is part of Khmer, and Σ is the collection of all Khmer words.

Example 2. Another natural example is English, with Σ the collection of all English words and L all the sentences and paragraphs written in English. However, English can also be represented as sentences in which each word is a letter of the English alphabet. We call this English L′, with Σ′={A,B,…,Z}. In terms of the meaning they contain, both L and L′ contain the same information. However, sentences in each of them are quite different. For example, the sentence "I Like Cats" is different in L and L′. In L it is the sequence of words I, Like, Cats, while in L′ it is the sequence I, L, I, K, E, C, A, T, S.

Example 3. Another example would be a collection of grey scale images. Each pixel is represented by a number between 0 and 255. We can view an image as a sequence of pixels, and in this view, an image is a sentence.

Example 4. Another example is the language L with vocabulary Σ={0,1,2,…,x,x2,…,+,−,=,(,)}. In this language you can write things like (1+x)(1−x)=1−x2 or something random such as x7−x. We can take L to be the set of correct formulae. This is an example of a language too.

Now, what is a language model? It is something that can produce sentences in L. A language model should be something that behaves like a human: it should consume a sentence and then speak back another sentence. Basically, it is a function M:Σ∗→Σ∗. We can build this map from a simpler function that consumes one sentence and produces only one word, m:Σ∗→Σ. To make m produce a sentence we do as follows. Take a sentence S0. The function m takes S0 and produces a word w in Σ, i.e. m(S0)=w. We glue w to S0 to get S1=S0w, and then feed S1 to m to get w′. We continue doing this a number of times. We can think of the whole process as M(S0)=ww′⋯w(n)=S′, which is a sentence too. This way of producing one word at a time is known as a recursive language model.

6. Loss Functions for Classification Task: Cross-Entropy

Setup: We have a set D=⋃i=1NDi as disjoint union of subsets Di . The function F:D→RN defined by F(x)=ei if x∈Di, where e1,e2,...,eN are the standard unit vectors, allow us to classify point in D based on which subset Di they are in. For each x, the vector value F(x) can be thought as a probability distribution on {D1,D2,...,DN}. To use neural network to do classification task means to find a neural network NN:D→RN that approximate F on D. The output NN(x)∈RN should be thought of as a probability distribution.

Now need a way to compare two probability distributions. This will allow us to compare how well a neural network does a classification job.

Definition

Let's P,Q:X→[0,1] be a probability distribution over X. The cross entropy H(P,Q) is defined as H(P,Q)=−∑x∈XP(x)log⁡(Q(x))

It would be cool if the cross entropy is a metric. However, it is not, one obvious thing is that it is not symmetric, ie H(P,Q)≠H(Q,P). What make the cross entropy a good candidate as a measure how close Q is to P is the following inequality H(P,Q)≥H(P,P) This means that the smaller we can make the cross entropy, the better we make Q close to P.

Proof Note that H(P,Q)=−∑x∈XP(x)log⁡Q(x) can be rewritten as H(P,Q)=−∑x∈X(P(x)log⁡Q(x)P(x)+P(x)log⁡P(x)) which simplifies to H(P,Q)=H(P,P)−∑x∈XP(x)log⁡Q(x)P(x) Now we need to prove that DKL(P‖Q)=∑x∈XP(x)log⁡P(x)Q(x)≥0. Note that DKL(P‖Q) is called the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence. It is 0 if and only if P=Q.

Now, log:R→R is a concave function, therefore it satisfies the Jensen's inequality: ∑i=1nαilog⁡(xi)≤log⁡(∑i=1nαixi) whenever xi∈[0,∞] and αi∈[0,1] satisfies ∑i=1nαi=1.

Applying this to the case where αi=P(xi) and xi=Q(xi)P(xi), we get: −DKL(P‖Q)≤log⁡(∑x∈XP(x)Q(x)P(x))=log⁡(1)=0 Thus, DKL(P‖Q)≥0.

Back to using neural networks NN to approximate probability distributions. We know that the output of the neural network is a vector NN(x)=(s1,s2,...,sN) in RN. This is not any probability distribution. To deal with this problem, we pass the result of the neural network into softmax function defined as:

Definition The function SoftMax:Rn→In is defined by SoftMax(x1,…,xn)=(p1,…,pn)=(ex1∑i=1nexi,…,exn∑i=1nexi)

For example, take x=(2,−1,0.5,3,−2)∈R5. First we take exi of each coordinate, which makes every coordinate positive, then we divide by their sum, so the pi add up to 1. The largest coordinate x4=3 gets the largest probability, and a negative coordinate still gets a small positive probability. You can drag the bars of x to see how SoftMax(x) changes.

7. Recurrent Neural Network

Imagine we have a collection of news articles C={A1,A2,...,AK} and we want to classify them into L={sport, politics, health}. Each news article is a string of words. To process these articles, we need a way to represent each words numerically so that we can use mathematical techniques to do the classification task.

Assume Ai=v1...vL where vk are words used to write Ai and L is the length of Ai. Let W={w1,w2,...,wN} be the set of vocabulary used to compose {A1,...,AK}, ordered in some manner. In the parlance of natural language processing, C is referred to as a corpus and W is the dictionary.

The goal is to represent wi numerically, one naive way to do this is to use number 1 to represent w1, 2 to represent w2, and so on. But the natural number has ordered structure, while we can't quite see that with words. So instead we should use vectors to represent words. More precisely, we want to find an embedding E:W→Rd for some d. One way to do this is to take d=|W|=N and send wi to the standard unit vector ei∈RN, this is known as the one hot encoding. However, there are several issue with this method. First, the embedding dimension is large, for example there are around 600000 words in English. Second, RN is a metric space, we would hope that that words wi and wj that are similar in meaning should be encoded closer compare to those that are not, but every pair of different words has distance 2 in the one-hot-encoding.

WR3e1=E(cat)e2=E(dog)e3=E(apple)E222

Continuous word embedding deal with the issues mentioned about the one hot encoding. There is d≪|W| and a map E:W→Rd that allow one to encoder each word as a vector where word with similar meaning stay close to one another. This is not a mathematical statement but rather an observed fact. We recommend the paper A Neural Probabilistic Language Model by Bengio et al for detail.

WR3E

The classification problem mention in the beginning now can be seen as classification of sequences of various length where each terms of the sequences are in Rd. A more general set up is having finite sequence x1,x2,...,xL in Rd, find a map f to the output space Y, which can be continuous or discrete. This is an example of time series analysis. To deal with time series, we introduce recurrent neural network.

7.1 Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)

The text A1=x1,x2,...,xLA1, where xi∈Rd. Any model that can classify this text should look at the whole text to do so. Let's try formulate this question of classifying text mathematically. Basically, we want a function f that take input as finite sequence in Rd to R3, such that if the sequence coming from sport article, healths, and politics, f would map it to e1,e2 and e3, respectively. We can not find such a function, what we can do is to approximate it.

One way to we can do is to train a several layers neural network that take the concatenation of xi, that is long vectors. However, here we run to the same problem of large dimensional space. The recurrent neural network was proposed to process sequence of any length and at the same time require relatively small number of parameters.

A recurrent neural network (RNN) processing the sequence x1,x2,...,xT is defined as follow {ht=f(xt,ht−1)yt=g(ht) for all 1≤t≤T, with ht∈RH for some H and h0=0. We should think of ht as the memory of the system up to time t and yt as the output. What happen is before anything happen, h0=0, the system contain no information, and at time t=1, the system look at the first word x1 and produce a memory. Next, it look at the second word x2 and use previous memory h1 to produce new memory h2. The process repeat until the end of the sequence. In the classification task we mention earlier, we would want to use yT to make prediction of the class the news article belong to. hT obtained by the system after it looks at all words that make up of A1.

We think of yt as the output of the network. And ht are known as hidden vector and H is called the hidden dimension.

To truly get the name neural network, f and g should be composition of affine maps and non-linear activation functions. One choice is the following {f(x,h)=σ(Wxx+Whh+bh)g(h)=Wyh+by Now we present a version of the universal approximation theorem of the RNN.

Theorem Let F1(x1),F2(x1,x2),...,FT(x1,..,xT) be continuous functions with xi∈A⊂Rd and their output are in Rm. If A is compact, then for any ε>0, there exist appropriate weight Wx,Wh,Wy,bh,by such that sup1≤t≤Tsupxi∈A|Ft(x1,..,xt)−yt|≤ε where yt is the output of the recurrent neural network with weights Wx,Wh,Wy,bh and by.

We will not prove this theorem here.

8. RNN Based Language Model

A language model is a function that takes sequence of words as input and output a new word. This allows one to get another new word using the word just generated and the previous word and one can keep produce as many word as one wants this way. This is called auto-regressive model.

In this section, we would build a character level language model based on RNN. What we mean is we would use one of the RNN model to process a sequence and use the hidden state to produce the resulting prediction.

The strategy is as follow. First we one hot encode each character, ie if the list of characters are {c1,c2,..,cK}, then one-hot(cj)=ej∈RK. Next we will project this embedding into another space Rd via a map E:RK→Rd, this process is called continuous embedding, and it can be done by multiplying ej by a matrix E, which is a learnable parameters. This whole process allow us to turn a sequence of character to a sequence of vectors in Rd, and from here we can use an RNN to approximate P(wn+1|w1,...,wn). This conditional probability is a map P:(w1,..,wn)→RK.

An RNN would be able to take arbitrarily length sequence and make prediction. If an RNN can learn to predict the next word based on a dependency of a long sequence, then it would be best. But we can't take too long a sequence, since the longer the sequence is, the more difficult for us to approximate the gradient, hence no effective learning.

The maximum length of sequence we choose to process is called block size. Now let's say we have block_size=32, this mean we want to use 32 character to predict the next characters. Let T be the text corpus we used for training. This mean during training, we take a chunk of 33 character piece of T, w1.....w32w33, use w1w2...w32 as input and w33 as output. The RNN goes through the embedding x1,x2,...,x32 of w1w2...w32 to produce h1,h2,...,h32, and we use h32 to predict w33 by map g:RH→RK defined by g(h)=SoftMax(Wyh+by).

Now if we want our model to take any sequence of length less than 32 to predict the next word, the data should be something like this x1 predict w2, x1x2 predict w3 and so on. And good news is we don't need to do more work for this, to compute h32, we already compute h1,h2,..., so what should do is apply g on these hidden vector. Now the input and output look like w1w2....w32 and w2.....w33, respectively, and the loss function is 132∑k=232H(ewk,g(hk−1)) Another thing to note is that we probably want to train a batch of data at the same time, this mean we should stable text at several places at time, and each place we would take 33 characters.

Next we want to talk about continuous embedding. Earlier, we mention that we should do one hot encoding and then map it to a low dimensional space. This is unnecessary in PyTorch. Let's me explain this. Say we have the text T=hello, then dictionary for this text is {e,h,l,o}, we can label e as 1, h as 2, l as 3 and o as 4, and the text is translated to 21334. Note that the vocabulary size is 4. The object nn.Embedding(4,3) take input of shape (batch_size,sequence_length) with each entry as "integer" and produce output of shape (batch_size, sequence_length,3=embedding_dimension). So basically, as soon as we encode a text as sequence of integers, we can feed it to nn.Embedding(4,3) to get continuous embedding. Note that 4 here is the size of the vocabulary.

# importing necessary package
import torch
import torch.nn as nn                                    #  this one is for neural network object
import torch.optim as optim                              #  this one is for optimizing algorithms 
import torch.nn.functional as F                          #  this one is used for functions like sigmoid and relu etc
import numpy 

#hyper parameter 
seq_length=30                                            
batch_size=32
device='gpu' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'     #  this tell the computer where the computation work
n_embd=128                                                #  this is for embedding dimension 
hidden_size=128                                         
num_layer=2                                              #  one can stack RNN on top of each other to create deep RNN
learning_rate=0.001
max_iters=10000                                          #  this is for the number of gradient descent we take
eval_interval=1000                                       #  the frequency which we evaluate the performance of the model
eval_iters=1000

The following text is a news article about Grothendieck by He was in mystic delirium’: was this hermit mathematician a forgotten genius whose ideas could transform AI – or a lonely madman? by The Guardian.

text="One day in September 2014, in a hamlet in the French Pyrenean foothills, Jean-Claude, a landscape gardener in his late 50s, was surprised to see his neighbour at the gate. He had not spoken to the 86-year-old in nearly 15 years after a dispute over a climbing rose that Jean-Claude had wanted to prune. The old man lived in total seclusion, tending to his garden in the djellaba he always wore, writing by night, heeding no one. Now, the long-bearded seeker looked troubled. Then, in 1970, in what he later called his great turning point, Grothendieck quit. Resigning from Frances elite Institut des Hautes Etudes Scientifiques IHES in protest at funding it received from the ministry of defence put an end to his high-level mathematics career. He occupied a few minor teaching posts until 1991, when he left his home underneath Provences Mont Ventoux and disappeared. No one friends, family, colleagues, the intimates who knew him as Shurik his childhood nickname, the Russian diminutive for Alexander knew where he was. Would you do me a favour he asked Jean-Claude. If I can. Could you buy me a revolver. Jean-Claude refused. Then, after watching the hermit who was deaf and nearly blind totter erratically about his garden, he telephoned the mans children. Even they had not spoken to their father in close to 25 years. When they arrived in the village of Lasserre, the recluse repeated his request for a revolver so he could shoot himself. There was barely room to move in his dilapidated house. The corridors were lined with shelves heaving with flasks of mouldering liquids. Overgrown plants spilled out of pots everywhere. Thousands of pages of arcane scrawling were lined up in canvas boxes in his library. But his infirmity had put paid to his studies, and he no longer saw any purpose in life. On 13 November, he died exhausted and alone in hospital in the neighbouring town of St-Lizier. The hermits name was Alexander Grothendieck. Born in 1928, he arrived in France from Germany as a refugee in 1939, and went on to revolutionise postwar mathematics as Einstein had physics a generation earlier. Moving beyond distinct disciplines such as geometry, algebra and topology, he worked in pursuit of a deeper, universal language to unify them all. At the heart of his work was a new conception of space, liberating it from the Euclidean tyranny of fixed points and bringing it into the 20th-century universe of relativity and probability. The flood of concepts and tools he introduced in the 1950s and 1960s awed his peers. Grothendiecks capacity for abstract thought is legendary. He rarely made use of specific equations to grasp at mathematical truths, instead intuiting the broader conceptual structure around them to make them surrender their solutions all at once. He compared the two approaches to using a hammer to crack a walnut versus soaking it patiently in water until it opens naturally. He was above all a thinker and a writer, who decided to apply his genius mostly to mathematics says Olivia Caramello, a 39-year-old Italian mathematician who is the leading proponent of his work today. His approach to mathematics was that of a philosopher, in the sense that the way in which one would prove results was more important to him than the results themselves. In Lasserre, he lived in near-complete solitude, with no television, radio, phone or internet. A handful of acolytes trekked up to the village once his whereabouts filtered out; he politely refused to receive most of them. When he did exchange words, he sometimes mentioned his true friends the plants. Wood, he believed, was conscious. He told Michel Camilleri, a local bookbinder who helped compile his writings, that his kitchen table knows more about you, your past, your present and your future than you will ever know. But these wild preoccupations took him to dark places he told one visitor that there were entities inside his house that might harm him. Grothendiecks genius defied his attempts at erasing his own renown. He lurks in the background of one of Cormac McCarthys final novels, Stella Maris, as an eminence grise who leads on its psychically disturbed mathematician protagonist. The long-awaited publication in 2022 of Grothendiecks exhaustive memoir, Harvests and Sowings, renewed interest in his work. And there is growing academic and corporate attention to how Grothendieckian concepts could be practically applied for technological ends. Chinese telecoms giant Huawei believes his esoteric concept of the topos could be key to building the next generation of AI, and has hired Fields medal-winner Laurent Lafforgue to explore this subject. But Grothendiecks motivations were not worldly ones, as his former colleague Pierre Cartier understood. Even in his mathematical milieu, he was not quite a member of the family writes Cartier. He pursued a kind of monologue, or rather a dialogue with mathematics and God, which to him were one and the same. Beyond his mathematics was the unknown. Were his final writings, an avalanche of 70000 pages in an often near-illegible hand, the aimless scribblings of a madman Or had the anchorite of Lasserre made one last thrust into the secret architecture of the universe And what would this outsider who had spurned the scientific establishment and modern society make of the idea of tech titans sizing up his intellectual property for exploitation In a famous passage from Harvests and Sowings, Grothendieck writes that most mathematicians work within a preconceived framework. They are like the inheritors of a large and beautiful house all ready-built, with its living rooms and kitchens and workshops, and its kitchen utensils and tools for all and sundry, with which there is indeed everything to cook and tinker. But he is part of a rarer breed the builders whose instinctive vocation and joy is to construct new houses. Now his son, Matthieu Grothendieck, is working out what to do with his fathers home. Lasserre lies on the top of a hill 22 miles 35km north of the Spanish border, in the remote Ariege departement, a haven for marginals, drifters and utopians. I first walk up there one piercingly cold January morning in 2023, mists cloaking forests of oak and beech, red kites surveying the fields in between. Grothendiecks home one of Laserrerres few three-storey houses, built by affluent dressmakers is at the villages southern extremity. Hanging above the road beyond are the snow-covered Pyrenees a promise of a higher reality. Matthieu answers the door wearing a dressing gown, with the sheepish air of a man emerging from hibernation. The 57-year-old has deeply creased features and a strong prow of a nose. Inheriting the house where his father experienced such mental ordeals weighs on him. This place has a history that is bigger than me he says, his voice softened by smoking. And as I have not got the means to knock it into shape, I feel bad about that. I feel as if I am still living in my fathers house. A former ceramicist, he is now a part-time musician. In the kitchen, a long framed scroll of Chinese script stands on a sideboard, next to one photograph of a Buddha sculpture and two of his mother, Mireille Dufour, whom Grothendieck left in 1972. Matthieu is her youngest child; he has a sister, Johanna, and brother, Alexandre. Grothendieck also had two other sons, Serge and John, with two other women. Above Matthieus bed is a garish portrait of his paternal grandfather, Alexander Schapiro, a Ukrainian Jewish anarchist who lost an arm escaping a tsarist prison, and later fought in the Spanish civil war. Schapiro and his partner, the German writer Johanna Grothendieck, left the five-year-old Grothendieck in foster care in Hamburg when they fled Nazi Germany in 1933 to fight for the socialist cause in Europe. He was reunited with his mother in 1939, and lived the remainder of the war in a French internment camp or in hiding. But his Jewish father, interned separately, was sent to Auschwitz and murdered on arrival in 1942. It was this legacy of abandonment, poverty and violence that drove the mathematician and finally overwhelmed him, Matthieu suggests. Artists and geniuses are making up for flaws and traumas. The wound that made Shurik a genius caught up with him at the end of his life. Matthieu leads me into the huge, broken-down barn behind the house. Heaped on the bare-earth floor is a mound of glass flasks encased in wicker baskets inside them are what remains of the mathematicians plant infusions, requiring hundreds of litres of alcohol. Far removed from conventional mathematics, Grothendiecks final studies were fixated on the problem of why evil exists in the world. His last recorded writing was a notebook logging the names of the deportees in his fathers convoy in August 1942. Matthieu believes his fathers plant distillations were linked with this attempt to explain the workings of evil a form of alchemy through which he was attempting to isolate different species properties of resilience to adversity and aggression. It is hard to understand says Matthieu. All I know is that they were not for drinking. Later, Matthieu agrees to let me look at his fathers Lasserre writings a cache of esoterica scanned onto hard disk by his daughter. At the start of 2023, the family were still negotiating their entry into the French national library. The writings have now been accepted and at some point will be publicly available for research. Serious scholarship is needed to decide their worth on mathematical, philosophical, and literary levels. I am definitely not qualified on the first count. I open a first page at random. The writing is spidery; there are occasional multicoloured topological diagrams, namechecks of past thinkers, often physicists Maxwell, Planck, Einstein and recurrent references to Satan and this cursed world. His children are struggling to fathom this prodigious output too. It is mystic but also down to earth. He talks about life with a form of moralism. It is completely out of fashion says Matthieu. But in my opinion there are pearls in there. He was the king of formulating things. After a couple of hours reading, head spinning, I feel the abyss staring into me. So imagine what it was like for Grothendieck. According to Matthieu, a friend once asked his father what his greatest desire was. The mathematician replied that this infernal circle of thought finally ceases. The colossal folds of Mont Ventouxs southern flank are mottled with April cloud shadow as cyclists skirt the mountain. In the Vaucluse departement of Provence, this is the terrain where Alexander Grothendieck took his first steps into mysticism. Now, another of his sons, Alexandre, lives in the area. I wander up a bumpy track to see the 62-year-old ambling out of oak woods, smiling, to meet me. Wearing a moth-eaten jumper, dark slacks, and slippers, Alexandre is slighter than his brother, with wind-chafed cheeks. He leads me into the giant hangar where he lives. It is piled with amps and instruments; at the back is a workshop where he makes kalimbas, a kind of African thumb piano. In 1980, his father moved a few kilometres to the west, to a house outside the village of Mormoiron. In the subsequent years, Grothendiecks thoughts turned inwards towards bewildering spiritual vistas. Even with all his wisdom and the depth of his insight, there was always a sense of excessiveness about my father says Alexandre. He always had to put himself in danger. He searched for it. Grothendieck had abandoned the commune he had been part of since 1973 in a village north of Montpellier, where he still taught at the university. From 1970 onwards, he had been one of Frances first radical ecologists and became increasingly preoccupied with meditation. In 1979, he spent a year dwelling intensely on his parents letters, a reflection that stripped away any lingering romanticism about them. The myth of their great love fell flat for Shurik it was a pure illusion says Johanna Grothendieck, who bears her grandmother's name. And he was able to decrypt all the traumatic elements of his childhood. He realised he had been quite simply abandoned by his own mother. This preoccupation with the past intensified into the mid-1980s, as Grothendieck worked on the manuscript for Harvests and Sowings. A reflection on his mathematical career, it was filled with stunning aphoristic insights, like the house metaphor. But, choked with David Foster Wallace-like footnotes, it was relentless and overwhelming too and steeped in a sense of betrayal by his former colleagues. In the wake of his revelations about his parents, this feeling became a kind of governing principle. It was a systematic thing with our papa to put someone on a pedestal, in order to see their flaws. Then bam they went down in flames says Alexandre. Although he still produced some mathematical work during this period, Grothendieck delved further into mysticism. He looked to his dreams as a conduit to the divine. He believed they were not products of his own psyche, but messages sent to him by an entity he called the Dreamer. This being was synonymous with God; as he conceived it, a kind of cosmic mother. Like a maternal breast, the grand dream offers us a thick and savorous milk, good to nourish and invigorate the soul he later wrote in The Key of Dreams, a treatise on the subject. Pierre Deligne, the brilliant pupil he accused in Harvests and Sowings of betraying him, felt his old master had lost his way. This was not the Grothendieck I admired he says, on the phone from Princetons Institute for Advanced Study. By summer 1989, the prophetic dreams had intensified into daily audiences, absorbing almost all of my time and energy with an angel Grothendieck called either Flora or Lucifera, depending on whether she manifested as benevolent or tormenting. She tutored him in a new cosmology, central to which was the question of suffering and evil in God's greater scheme. He believed, for example, that the speed of light being close to, but not precisely, 300000km a second, was evidence of Satans interference. He was in a form of mystic delirium says another former pupil, Jean Malgoire, now a professor at Montpellier University. Which is also a form of mental illness. It would have been good if he could have been seen by a psychiatrist at that point. In real life, he had become forbidding and remote. Matthieu spent two months in Mormoiron working on the house. During that time, his father invited him in only once. His son blew his top. He had lost interest in others. I could no longer feel any authentic or sincere empathy. But Grothendieck was still interested in people's souls. On 26 January 1990, he sent 250 of his acquaintances including his children a messianic, seven-page typed epistle, entitled Letter of the Good News. He announced a date 14 October 1996 for the Day of Liberation when evil on Earth would cease, and said they had been chosen to help usher in the new era. It was a kind of remake of the most limited aspects of Christianity says Johanna."
vocabs=sorted(set(text))
char_to_idx={char:idx for idx,char in enumerate(vocabs)}  # translate from character to index based on vocabs
idx_to_char={idx:char for idx,char in enumerate(vocabs)}  # translate from  index 
encode= lambda s: [char_to_idx[char] for char in s]       # this is a function that convert a sequence of chars to seq of integers
decode= lambda l: ''.join(idx_to_char[idx] for idx in l)  # convert a sequence of integers to sequence of chars
data=torch.tensor(encode(text),dtype=torch.long)          # used function encode to turn the whole text to a sequence of integer
n=int(0.8*len(text))                                      # we make a cut to get part of the data for training and for testing
train_data=data[:n]                                       # this is part of the data used for training
val_data=data[n:]                                         # this is part of the data used for testing, unseen by during training
vocab_size=len(vocabs)

# We create a function that catch a batch of data for stochastic gradient descent
def get_batch(split):   
    data=train_data if split == 'train' else val_data      # there are two type of data, from train_data and from val_data
    idx=torch.randint(len(data)-seq_length, (batch_size,)) # this produces an array of size (batch_size) of random integers 
    x=torch.stack([data[i:i+seq_length] for i in idx])     # get a batch of input data
    y=torch.stack([data[i+1:i+seq_length+1] for i in idx]) # get a batch of output data
    x,y=x.to(device),y.to(device)                          # move x and y to device
    return x,y

For example, take seq_length=6 and batch_size=3, and suppose torch.randint gives the starting places i=4,13,30. Then x and y are the following.

@torch.no_grad()
def estimate_loss():
    out = {}
    model.eval()  # Set model to evaluation mode
    for split in ['train', 'val']:                      # there are 2 type of loss, one for train_data and one for val_data
        losses = torch.zeros(eval_iters)                # create tensor to hold losses for each sample
        for k in range(eval_iters):                     # we compute loss for eval_iters batches of data
            X, Y = get_batch(split)                     # get batch of data
            logits, loss = model(X, Y)                  # forward pass
            losses[k] = loss.item()                     # store the loss for each batch of data
        out[split] = losses.mean().item()               # compute the mean loss after the loop
    model.train()                                       # set model back to training mode
    return out
class RNNLanguageModel(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):                                    # attribute part of the data
        super().__init__()                                 # initialize the model
        self.embd_table = nn.Embedding(vocab_size, n_embd) # continuous embedding
        self.lstm = nn.LSTM(n_embd, hidden_size, num_layers=num_layer, batch_first=True) # we use LSTM instead of vanilla RNN
        self.proj = nn.Linear(hidden_size, vocab_size)     # this is the function g:R^h to R^vocab_size before the softmax

    def forward(self, idx, targets=None):                  # during inference, we don't need target. The model take idx as input
        B, T = idx.shape                                   # get_batch produce idx of the shape (batch_size, sequence_length)   
        tok_emb = self.embd_table(idx)                     # turn index to continuous embedding
        output, _ = self.lstm(tok_emb)                     # the LSTM processes sequence of vectors input, out=sequence of h_t
        logits = self.proj(output)                         # project h_t to prepare for softmax
        
        if targets is None:  # Corrected variable name     # if this is during inference, ie no target
            loss = None
        else:                                              # if during training, we use to logits to compute cross-entropy
            B, T, C = logits.shape                         
            logits = logits.view(B * T, C)                 # there are B*T prediction that logits make
            targets = targets.view(B * T)                  # there are B*T ground truth
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, targets)        
        
        return logits,loss

    def generate(self, idx, generate_length, seq_length):      # this are the input for generating an output
        hidden = None                                          # ensure that first hidden state h_0,c_0=0
        for _ in range(generate_length):                
            idx_cond = idx[:, -seq_length:]                    # use at most seq_length argument as input for LSTM
            tok_emb = self.embd_table(idx_cond)            
            output, hidden = self.lstm(tok_emb, hidden)
            logits = self.proj(output[:, -1, :])               # select the last hidden state and project it to get logits
            probs = F.softmax(logits, dim=-1)                  # apply softmax on logits along the last dimension
            idx_next = torch.multinomial(probs, num_samples=1) # select next index according to probability distribution prob
            idx = torch.cat((idx, idx_next), dim=1)            # add the prediction to the list of output 
        generated_text=decode(idx[0].tolist())
        return generated_text
model=RNNLanguageModel()                                       # this initialize a model
total_params = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)
print(f"Total trainable parameters: {total_params}")
print(f"The text length is {len(text)}")
print(f"The ratio of parameters to text is {total_params/len(text):.4f}")

optimizer = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=learning_rate)
for iter in range(max_iters):
    # every once in a while evaluate the loss on train and val sets
    if iter % eval_interval == 0 or iter == max_iters - 1:
        losses = estimate_loss()
        print(f"step {iter}: train loss {losses['train']:.4f}, val loss {losses['val']:.4f}")
    # sample a batch of data
    xb, yb = get_batch('train')
    # evaluate the loss
    logits, loss = model(xb, yb)
    optimizer.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

8.1 The n-gram Language Model

We've seen that the RNN model earlier attempts to approximate P(wL+1|w1,...,wL). Another way to get this probability distribution is to actually count it, since this is a finite system. This is known as the n-gram model. Allow me to explain the 3-gram model and then you'll understand the n-gram model. Let's say we want to predict the next word based on 3 words before it that imitates a text T, ie T is the training data. First, we can ask what the possible combination of 3 words are. If the text T is based on 1000 words, then there are 10003 possible of 3 words sentences. Next for each of the combination w1w2w3, we count its occurrence in the text, and count what are the word that come after it and in what frequency, from here we can compute the exact probability.

Below is a short text. A window of two words slides along it, and every time it reads "the cat", we count the word that comes after. Dividing by the number of times "the cat" appears gives the probability of each next word, which is one row of the 2-gram model. The table after it has the rows for all the pairs of words in the text.

the cat likes fish . the dog likes milk . the cat likes milk . the cat eats fish . the dog eats meat . the cat sleeps . the dog likes the cat . the cat likes the dog . a cat eats fish . a dog sleeps .

Our goal here is not to study the n-gram model itself, but to use it to help us understand better what the RNN and other language model does.

Now what are some of the problem encounter by the n-gram model? First, one main issue is that the n-gram model would give uniform distribution for any sequence of words that doesn't appear in the text. Consider creating an 2-gram model based on a text that the sequence cat loves doesn't exist, when we ask the model to predict what word come next after this sequence, it will predict anything can happen with equal probability. We don't want something like that. The RNN model takes input as sequence of vectors, and it can process any sequence, so it doesn't face the problem that n-gram model has. One way one hope the RNN give good prediction is as follow: During embedding, as the model look through the text, it learns that the embedding of the word like and love are close, and it has seen the sequence cat likes in the text, this allow us to give a non-uniform distribution for the P(.|cat loves) based on what it seen for cat likes. One question one can ask is does the RNN do more than a modification of the n-gram model? By modified RNN here we mean something like this: the model first regroup all possible 3 words sentences based on their similar meaning and then does the 3-gram model on that.

The hope here is that the embedding learned during the training of the RNN is a way that allows us to embed each word in Rd, making words with similar meaning to be nearby.
